chunks.title: Soil is the loose top
chunks.text: Soil is the loose top layer of the earth where plants grow. It is made from rock that has broken into tiny bits over thousands of years, mixed with the rotted remains of dead plants and animals. The dark crumbly part that comes from rotted plants is called humus, and it is what makes soil rich. Soil also holds water and air in the small gaps between its bits. A plant sends its roots down into those gaps to drink water and to hold itself steady. Good soil is alive, full of worms and insects and countless tiny living things you cannot see.

The dark crumbly part that comes from rotted plants is called humus, and it is what makes soil rich.

chunks.title: Different soils suit different crops,
chunks.text: Different soils suit different crops, and India has many kinds. Sandy soil has big grains, so water drains through it fast and it dries quickly. Clay soil has very fine grains, holds water for a long time, and turns sticky when it is wet. Loam is a mixture of sand and clay, and most crops grow best in it. The black soil of the Deccan plateau holds moisture well and is famous for cotton. The flat plains beside the Ganga and other great rivers have alluvial soil, dropped there by the rivers over many floods, and it is some of the most fertile land in the country.

chunks.title: A seed is a tiny
chunks.text: A seed is a tiny plant packed with its own lunch. Inside the hard seed coat there is a baby plant, and beside it a store of food to live on until the plant can feed itself. When you split a soaked gram or a peanut into two halves, those halves are the food store. When a seed gets what it needs it begins to grow, and that is called germination. First a small root pushes down into the soil, then a shoot pushes up, and only when the first green leaves open does the young plant start making food of its own.

chunks.title: Seeds do not need sunlight
chunks.text: Seeds do not need sunlight to sprout, and this surprises many people. What a seed needs is water to soften it and wake it up, air to breathe, and warmth. That is why seeds sprout under the soil in the dark, and why sprouted moong grows in a damp covered cloth in the corner of a kitchen. Sunlight becomes important later, once the shoot is above the ground and the green leaves begin their work. A seed buried too deep may use up its stored food before it reaches the light, so most seeds are sown only a little way under the surface.

chunks.title: Roots do two jobs for
chunks.text: Roots do two jobs for a plant. They grip the soil so the plant is not blown over, and they drink in water along with the minerals dissolved in it. Some plants have one thick main root going straight down with smaller roots branching off it, like gram, mustard and carrot. Others have a bunch of thin roots of about the same size spreading out sideways, like wheat, maize and grass. Roots grow towards water. A field wetted only on the surface grows shallow roots, while deeper watering encourages roots to reach down, where they can survive a dry spell.

chunks.title: Manure and compost put back
chunks.text: Manure and compost put back into the soil what a crop takes out. Cow dung, dry leaves, straw and vegetable peels are piled up and left to rot for some weeks, and tiny living things break them down into a dark crumbly material. Mixed into a field it feeds the soil, holds water like a sponge, and keeps the ground soft. Factory made fertiliser works faster because it supplies plant nutrients directly, but it adds no humus, and using far more than the crop needs wastes money and can spoil the soil and the water nearby. Many farmers use both, and use them carefully.

chunks.title: Irrigation means giving crops water
chunks.text: Irrigation means giving crops water when the rain does not. In India water is lifted from open wells and tube wells, carried across the fields in canals from a dam, or stored in village tanks and ponds through the dry months. The oldest method is to flood the field, letting water run along channels between the rows. Flooding is simple, but much of the water sinks away or dries up before the roots can use it. How much water a crop needs changes with the crop, the soil and the weather, so a farmer waters more often on sandy soil than on heavy clay.

chunks.title: Drip irrigation delivers water drop
chunks.text: Drip irrigation delivers water drop by drop through thin pipes laid along the rows, right at the base of each plant. Because the water goes straight to the roots and very little dries away, a field can be grown with a fraction of the water that flooding needs. Sprinklers throw water over the crop like light rain, which suits some crops and uneven ground. Too much water brings its own trouble. Land that stays soaked pushes air out of the soil so roots cannot breathe, and when that water dries it can leave salt behind that makes the field harder to farm.

chunks.title: The monsoon decides the farming
chunks.text: The monsoon decides the farming year across most of India. From about June to September, moist winds blow in from the sea and bring the heavy rain that fills wells, tanks and rivers. Crops sown with the first rains and harvested after the monsoon ends are called kharif crops, and they include rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut and tur dal. These are planted when the soil is warm and wet. A monsoon that arrives late, or stops in the middle, can leave a whole district short of grain, which is why farmers watch the June sky so closely.

chunks.title: Rabi crops are the winter
chunks.text: Rabi crops are the winter crops, sown from about October to December and harvested in March and April. Wheat, gram, mustard, peas and barley are the main ones. They grow through the cool months when there is little rain, so they lean on moisture stored in the soil and on irrigation. Clear days and cold nights suit wheat well. Between the rabi harvest and the next monsoon, a farmer with water to spare may raise a short summer crop such as watermelon, cucumber, or green fodder for the cattle.

chunks.title: Weather and climate are not
chunks.text: Weather and climate are not the same thing. Weather is what the sky is doing right now. It is the heat, the wind, the clouds and the rain of this morning or this week, and it can change in an hour. Climate is the usual pattern of weather at a place, worked out over very many years. Saying that Rajasthan is hot and dry is a statement about climate. Saying that it rained in Jaisalmer yesterday is a statement about weather. A farmer chooses the crop for the year to suit the climate, then adjusts week by week to suit the weather.
chunks.explain: Weather and climate are not the same thing. Weather is what the sky is doing right now. It is the heat, the wind, the clouds and the rain of this morning or this week, and it can change in an hour.

chunks.title: Ploughing loosens the top layer
chunks.text: Ploughing loosens the top layer of a field before sowing. A plough, pulled by bullocks or by a tractor, cuts into the ground and turns the soil over so the hard baked crust is broken up. Loosened soil lets air reach the roots, lets rain soak in instead of running off, and lets tender young roots push through easily. Turning the soil also buries weeds and mixes in manure. After ploughing, the lumps are broken and the surface is levelled, so that water spreads evenly instead of collecting in low spots and drowning part of the crop.

Loosened soil lets air reach the roots, lets rain soak in instead of running off, and lets tender young roots push through easily.

chunks.title: Sowing is the placing of
chunks.text: Sowing is the placing of seed in the prepared field, and the way it is done matters. Scattering seed by hand is quick but uneven, so some patches come up crowded and others stay bare. A seed drill, pulled behind a tractor or a pair of bullocks, drops seed in neat lines at the same depth and covers it over. Even spacing gives every plant its share of sunlight, water and room for its roots. Plants crowded together fight one another and all stay small. Depth matters too, because seed left lying on top is eaten by birds.

A seed drill, pulled behind a tractor or a pair of bullocks, drops seed in neat lines at the same depth and covers it over.

chunks.title: Weeds are simply plants growing
chunks.text: Weeds are simply plants growing where the farmer does not want them. They are usually tough and fast growing, and they steal the water, the light and the nutrients meant for the crop. A field left unweeded can lose a large part of its harvest without any insect or disease being involved at all. Weeds are pulled out by hand, scraped out with a khurpi or a hoe, or killed with chemical weedicides. Ploughing before sowing destroys many of them early, and a crop sown thick enough to shade the ground leaves weeds little room to start.

A field left unweeded can lose a large part of its harvest without any insect or disease being involved at all.

chunks.title: Pests are the animals and
chunks.text: Pests are the animals and insects that damage a crop. Caterpillars chew the leaves, stem borers tunnel inside the stalks of rice and sugarcane, aphids suck the juice from soft young shoots, and rats and birds take grain from the field and from the store. A swarm of locusts can strip a green field bare in a few hours. Damage is worst when the same crop is grown in the same field season after season, because the pests that like that crop build up in the soil and in the stubble, ready and waiting for the next one.

A swarm of locusts can strip a green field bare in a few hours.

chunks.title: Controlling pests need not mean
chunks.text: Controlling pests need not mean spraying poison. Many farmers plant a different crop the next season so that the pests which were building up have nothing to feed on. Neem leaves and neem oil have long been used to keep certain insects away. Birds, spiders, frogs and ladybird beetles eat huge numbers of crop pests at no cost at all. Chemical pesticides do work, but they kill helpful creatures too, and they are dangerous to people. They must be handled only by trained adults with proper covering, and children should never open, carry or play near them.

chunks.title: Most insects in a field
chunks.text: Most insects in a field are not pests at all, and that is worth remembering before anybody reaches for a spray. Bees and butterflies carry pollen from flower to flower, and without those visits many crops set far fewer fruits and seeds. Ladybird beetles eat aphids by the hundred. Spiders and dragonflies eat the insects that eat the crop. When a field is sprayed heavily the helpers die first, because there were fewer of them to begin with, and the pests often come back stronger than before with nothing left to hunt them.

chunks.title: Growing pulses puts goodness back
chunks.text: Growing pulses puts goodness back into a field. Gram, moong, tur, peas and groundnut belong to a family of plants that carry tiny lumps called nodules on their roots. Inside those nodules live bacteria that take nitrogen out of the air and turn it into a form plants can use, and some of it stays behind in the soil. So a field that grows a pulse crop one season is richer for the wheat or the rice that follows. Changing the crop from season to season is called crop rotation, and it feeds the soil while it starves the pests.

chunks.title: Earthworms are the quiet workers
chunks.text: Earthworms are the quiet workers of a healthy field. They swallow soil along with dead leaves, and what passes out of them is a fine rich material that plants grow well in. Their tunnels open up the ground so that air and rainwater travel downwards instead of sitting on the surface. A field full of earthworms is usually a field with plenty of rotted plant matter in it, because that is their food. Heavy chemical use, and soil left bare to bake in the sun, drive them away, and that soil slowly becomes hard and lifeless.

chunks.title: Harvesting is the cutting of
chunks.text: Harvesting is the cutting of a crop once the grain is ripe and dry enough. Cut too early and the grain is soft and shrivels. Cut too late and it drops to the ground or is spoiled by a late shower. After cutting comes threshing, which separates the grain from the stalks by beating them or by running a machine over them. Then comes winnowing. The mixture is poured slowly from a height in a breeze, so the light husk blows aside while the heavier grain falls straight down into a clean pile.

chunks.title: Storing grain safely matters as
chunks.text: Storing grain safely matters as much as growing it. Grain put away even slightly damp will grow fungus, smell musty and become unfit to eat, so it is first spread out and dried well in the sun. Then it goes into closed metal bins, sealed drums or lined pits that rats and insects cannot enter and that keep the monsoon damp out. Farmers have long mixed in dried neem leaves to discourage insects. Every kilo lost in the store is a kilo grown for nothing, so a good store is quietly worth as much as a good harvest.

chunks.title: Sprouting a seed in a
chunks.text: Sprouting a seed in a tin can shows the whole story in miniature. Fill the can with soil, push two or three gram or moong seeds about a centimetre down, and sprinkle enough water to keep the soil damp but never soaked. In two or three days the seed splits and a pale root appears. In a week there is a small green shoot. Water it too much and it rots for want of air. Keep it in a dark cupboard and it grows tall, thin and sickly. A tin can teaches the same lessons as a whole field, only faster.
